newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine vice-president calls for "Evita" boycott.
newsitem.headline: Argentine vice-president calls for "Evita" boycott.

text.p: British filmmaker Alan Parker's "Evita" was headed for a stormy opening in local theatres this week after Argentine Vice-President Carlos Ruckauf called on Monday for a boycott of the movie musical.

"Just as Parker has the right to make a film ... I have the right to propose that people don't go see it," Ruckauf said. He described the film as "clearly offensive" and an insult to the memory of the legendary Eva Peron, Argentina's best-loved political icon, but he acknowledged having seen only video clips of "Evita," which stars pop singer Madonna.

"It's very ignorant of (Ruckauf) to say anything before he sees it," Parker told a Buenos Aires news conference on Monday. He said President Carlos Menem had commended him for the awards won by the film that opens in Buenos Aires on Thursday. "I got a letter from Menem congratulating me for winning the Golden Globe awards and I spoke to (presidential chief of staff Alberto) Kohan on Friday, who wished me well."

"Evita" got lukewarm reviews after Friday's press premiere attended by Parker, with critics questioning its historical accuracy. It also revived debate over the original Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Weber stage musical's portrayal of the wife of former President Juan Domingo Peron as a woman who used her sex appeal to win power and manipulate the masses.

But Parker insisted the movie was unbiased. "I honestly tried to make a balanced film but I understand it would be impossible to please everyone," he said, noting that Eva Peron was regarded among Argentines as either a saint or a sinner.
"The most important thing about the subject is that people don't agree at all -- it's at the heart of why it's such an incredibly interesting story," Parker said.

The filmmaker fielded questions from reporters often as hostile as Ruckauf, who had earlier urged a boycott of the film, saying that paying for a ticket was a way of helping Parker "make millions by insulting a figure like Evita."

"I think I was very respectful of her ... Here in Argentina some people think I've been too critical, while in other places they say I glorified the woman," Parker said. He said "Evita" was the most difficult film of his career, which includes "Midnight Express", "The Wall" and "Birdy."
Parker defended his choice of Madonna for the title role and said that while he was disappointed the movie did not win major Oscar nominations he was not overly concerned.
